title: The Corner Store's Arithmetic
body: The bell above the door jingles. A man in a grease-stained jacket drops a five-dollar bill on the counter. 'Pack of Reds and a lottery ticket,' he says. I scan the cigarettes. The register reads $7.15. He frowns. 'I thought they were six bucks now.' 'Price went up last week,' I say. He sighs, pulls out a worn wallet, and starts counting out coins. Two quarters. Three dimes. A nickel. Four pennies. He places them on the counter one by one. The total is $7.19. He's four cents short. 'You got a penny?' I ask. He pats his pockets again, produces a single copper coin, and slaps it down. The transaction is complete. I hand him his change. A dollar and eighty-six cents. He pockets it without looking. The lottery ticket prints with a satisfying whir. This is the corner store's economy. It runs on exact change and the quiet friction of small transactions. People think a corner store is a place of impulse buys, but really, it's a lesson in precision. The price tag tells the truth. The customer's wallet tells the truth. And the register, well, the register just keeps a perfect count. A woman comes in for a single can of cat food. She has a dollar and fifty cents in quarters. She counts them twice, just to be sure. 'Boring wins,' I think to myself. There's no free lunch here. Every item has a cost. Every coin has a value. And every transaction, no matter how small, is a complete equation. I watch the street outside through the dusty window. A kid drops a dollar on the sidewalk. Someone picks it up. A fair trade. The man with the lottery ticket is already halfway down the block, the smoke from his cigarette trailing behind him. The bell jingles again as the next customer walks in. The cycle continues. The arithmetic never stops.
